title: The Inheritance of Judah
summary: Judah receives the first and largest allotment west of the Jordan. The chapter traces its borders from the Dead Sea to the Mediterranean and from the wilderness of Zin to the Valley of Hinnom, tells how Caleb took Hebron and Debir and how his daughter Acsah asked for springs of water, and lists the towns of Judah by region. It ends by admitting that Judah could not drive out the Jebusites of Jerusalem.
story: Caleb's claim in chapter 14 leads straight into the allotment of his tribe. Judah comes first among the western tribes, as it had led the march in the wilderness (Numbers 10:14), and its territory takes up the whole south of the land. Judah's prominence looks forward: Jacob had blessed Judah with the promise that the scepter would not depart from him (Genesis 49:10), and from this territory would come David, the kings of Jerusalem, and in time Jesus of Bethlehem. The chapter also carries two short stories, Caleb and Othniel's victories and Acsah's request, that reappear in Judges 1, and it closes with a warning note about Jerusalem that will not be resolved until David takes the city in 2 Samuel 5.
historical:
Judah's borders enclose some of the most varied land in the region. The eastern border is the Dead Sea (here the Salt Sea). The southern border runs through the dry country near Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Egypt, usually identified with the Wadi el-Arish in northern Sinai. The northern border climbs from the Jordan past Achor and En-rogel, skirts the southern edge of Jerusalem along the Valley of Hinnom, and runs west past Beth-shemesh to the coast. The Valley of Hinnom later became notorious for child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31), and its name, in the form Gehenna, became a word for the place of final judgment in the teaching of Jesus.

The town list includes places that play later roles: Ziklag, given to David by the Philistine king Achish (1 Samuel 27:6); Keilah, which David rescued (1 Samuel 23); En-gedi, the oasis by the Dead Sea where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 24); and Lachish and Azekah, the last fortified towns of Judah to hold out against Babylon (Jeremiah 34:7). Ostraca (inscribed pottery pieces) found at Lachish in the 1930s include a letter from about that time mentioning Azekah. The lists are grouped into districts, and scholars debate their origin. Albrecht Alt and others argued that they reflect the administrative districts of the later kingdom of Judah; others hold that they preserve older tribal records, updated over time.
cultural:
Borders in the ancient world were drawn by landmarks: springs, ridges, valleys, stones, and towns, as in this chapter. A town and its villages (verse 32 and throughout) formed a unit, with a walled town serving as a refuge and market for unwalled farming settlements around it. Water was the key to life in the Negev, the dry southern region. Acsah's request makes perfect sense there: land without springs was nearly worthless, and she asked her father for a gift that would make her inheritance livable.

Offering a daughter in marriage to the man who conquered a city was a way of honoring and rewarding a champion, as Saul later promised his daughter to whoever killed Goliath (1 Samuel 17:25). The story also shows a daughter taking initiative: Acsah urges her husband, then makes the request herself. Her father's question, "What do you desire?", and his generous answer present a picture of a family in which a daughter could ask and receive.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1-12 trace the boundaries in a clockwise sweep: south, east, north, and west. Verses 13-19 insert the Caleb story, continuing chapter 14. Verses 20-62 list the towns in groups by region: the Negev (verses 21-32), the foothills or Shephelah (verses 33-47), the hill country (verses 48-60), and the wilderness by the Dead Sea (verses 61-62), with running totals after each group. The totals do not always match the number of names given (verse 32, for example), probably because some names are compound or the list was updated in transmission. Verse 63 closes the chapter on a sober note that stands against the fullness of everything before it.

outline.t: The eastern, northern, and western borders
Towns of the foothills and coast
Towns of the wilderness, and Jerusalem not taken

doctrines.note: The long list of borders and towns is the promise to Abraham made concrete. God's gift is not vague spiritual space but land with springs, valleys, and villages, where real families will live.

Acsah's story shows a father generous to his daughter and a daughter free to ask. She receives "a blessing" in the form of water for her land, a small picture of how a household can reflect God's generosity.
Verse 63 is the first of several notes that the tribes did not drive out the peoples of the land. Judges 1 will show how these unfinished tasks became a snare.

words.note: Gevul, border or boundary. Used twenty-three times in this chapter, it marks the land as defined and given. Old Testament law forbade moving a neighbor's boundary marker (Deuteronomy 19:14), because boundaries protected the inheritance God had given each family.

Berakah, blessing. Acsah asks her father, "Give me a blessing," and the blessing turns out to be springs of water. In the Old Testament a blessing is often concrete: life, fruitfulness, land, and water, all gifts that make flourishing possible.
Yarash, to take possession by driving out. Caleb drove out the sons of Anak (verse 14), but Judah could not drive out the Jebusites (verse 63). The same verb frames both success and failure.

Chatser, village or settlement. The phrase "along with their villages" recurs after each group of towns. It reminds the reader that the inheritance included the small farming communities where most Israelites actually lived.

christ: Judah's allotment is the ground on which the royal line of David will grow, and so the line toward the Messiah. Bethlehem, though not named in the Hebrew list here, lay in Judah's hill country, and Micah 5:2 promised that a ruler would come from it, a text Matthew 2:6 applies to Jesus. The New Testament calls Jesus the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5). Jerusalem, left in Jebusite hands at the end of this chapter, would later become David's city and the place where Jesus was crucified and raised. The chapter itself makes no prediction; it lays down the geography on which the later story will be played out.
questions: Acsah boldly asked her father for what her land needed. How freely do you ask God for what you need, and what holds you back?
Judah's inheritance was large and detailed, yet Jerusalem remained untaken. Where in your life does a great gift sit alongside something left undone?
Why do you think the Bible preserves long lists of towns and borders? What might they have meant to the families who lived in those places?
